items.title: Topological manifolds without boundary
Manifold charts, coordinate domains, and coordinate functions
The coordinate representation of a map
Smoothly compatible charts
Smooth chart compatibility is symmetric and reflexive
items.strategy: Reflexivity is immediate from the identity transition map. Symmetry is not hidden in bijectivity: it uses the two-sided clause in the compatibility definition exactly as stated.

items.title: Smooth atlases
The union of two compatible smooth atlases is a smooth atlas
items.strategy: Check that cross-chart compatibility is the only extra condition beyond the two given atlas conditions. Once every chart in one atlas is compatible with every chart in the other, pairwise compatibility for the union follows immediately.

items.title: Compatibility of smooth atlases is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Use the previous lemma to package transitivity at the atlas level. The proof avoids pretending that chartwise compatibility is transitive without a covering argument.

items.title: All charts compatible with a smooth atlas form a smooth atlas
items.strategy: At a point of overlap between two new charts, choose a chart from the reference atlas and factor the new transition through that chart. Smoothness is local, so the chain rule turns compatibility with the atlas into compatibility with each other.

items.title: The smooth structure generated by an atlas
Each smooth atlas is contained in a unique maximal smooth atlas
items.strategy: The previous lemma gives existence of the atlas of all compatible charts. Uniqueness comes from maximality, and the same argument shows that two atlases determine the same smooth structure exactly when their union is again a smooth atlas.

items.title: Smooth manifolds
An open subset of a smooth manifold has a canonical restricted smooth structure
items.strategy: Restrict each chart to the open trace. These restricted charts still cover the subspace, their transition maps are inherited from the ambient ones, and the maximal-atlas theorem removes dependence on the presenting atlas.

items.title: Open subsets of Euclidean space have the standard smooth structure
items.strategy: Use the identity chart on the Euclidean open set. Every compatible chart has smooth transitions with that identity chart, so the resulting maximal atlas is exactly the standard one.

items.title: Products of smooth manifolds have a canonical product smooth structure
items.strategy: Take products of charts and write the transition maps blockwise. The product universal property and the Euclidean product topology identify the local models, while the transition maps are smooth componentwise.

items.title: Countable disjoint unions of fixed-dimensional smooth manifolds are smooth manifolds
items.strategy: Use the disjoint-union topology and the component charts from each summand. Countability is the point: it lets the union of the countable chart bases remain countable, so second countability is preserved.

items.title: $C^r$ and smooth maps between smooth manifolds
Chart independence of $C^r$ smoothness
items.strategy: Change source and target charts by composing with transition diffeomorphisms on the left and right. The Euclidean chain rule shows that if one coordinate representative is $C^r$, then every other one is too.

items.title: Smooth maps are continuous
items.strategy: A smooth coordinate representative is in particular $C^1$, hence continuous. Compose with the chart homeomorphisms and use locality on the source to lift continuity to the manifold map.

items.title: Identity maps and composites of smooth maps are smooth
items.strategy: The coordinate formula for a composite is the composite of coordinate formulas on the correct overlap restriction. The Euclidean chain rule gives smoothness once the domains are written out honestly.

items.title: Diffeomorphisms and local diffeomorphisms of manifolds
Chart maps are diffeomorphisms onto Euclidean open sets
items.strategy: A smooth chart belongs to the maximal atlas, so every transition between that chart and itself or another smooth chart is smooth in both directions. The chart map and its inverse are therefore smooth by the very definition of smooth structure.

items.title: Smoothness is local on the source
items.strategy: If a map is smooth on an open cover, then around each point one of those open sets supplies the needed chart pair. The chart-independence lemma then turns that local witness into a chart-independent smoothness statement.

items.title: Smooth maps paste over an open cover
items.strategy: First use the topological pasting lemma to get a well-defined continuous map. Then apply smoothness locality on the source to each open set of the cover.

items.title: A map into a product is smooth iff its components are smooth
items.strategy: Write product charts componentwise and identify the coordinate representative with the product of the component representatives. The product universal property turns the manifold statement into the Euclidean componentwise one.

items.title: A map from a disjoint union is smooth iff each restriction is smooth
items.strategy: On a disjoint union, every point lies in exactly one summand, so smoothness is checked there. The coproduct universal property packages the converse statement about maps assembled from the restrictions.

items.title: Restrictions, corestrictions, and products of smooth maps are smooth
items.strategy: Each construction is a direct application of the earlier locality, composition, and product criteria once the openness hypotheses are stated explicitly.

items.title: A smooth map with everywhere smooth local inverses is a local diffeomorphism
items.strategy: By hypothesis each point has neighborhoods on which the map has a smooth inverse. The local inverses agree where both are defined, because both are inverse to the same map on the overlap, so the local-diffeomorphism condition follows directly.

items.title: Coordinate balls form a basis of a topological manifold
items.strategy: Inside a chart image, choose an ordinary Euclidean ball around the coordinate point with compact closure still inside the image. Pulling such balls back through the chart produces a neighborhood basis in the manifold.

items.title: Topological manifolds are locally compact and locally path connected
items.strategy: Transport the Euclidean local compactness and polygonal connectedness of open balls through coordinate charts. The coordinate-ball basis keeps both properties local at every point.

items.title: Components of a topological manifold are open and at most countable
items.strategy: Local path connectedness makes components of open sets open, hence manifold components open. A countable basis then injects the family of components into the basis by sending each component to its first basis element.

items.title: Topological manifolds are sigma-compact
items.strategy: Start from a fixed countable basis of coordinate balls whose closures are compact. The chart-basis lemma already gives those compact-closure basis elements directly, so enumerating their closures yields a countable compact cover with no pointwise choice.

items.title: Topological manifolds are metrizable and paracompact
items.strategy: Use the published topology route recorded in the design: locally compact Hausdorff implies regularity, second countability implies Lindelof, regular Lindelof implies paracompact, and second-countable regular spaces are metrizable by the Urysohn theorem. This avoids the stronger Stone-first route the design explicitly rejected.

items.title: Manifold conventions and the role of second countability
Hausdorff and locally Euclidean do not by themselves make a manifold
items.strategy: Use the long line. It is Hausdorff and locally homeomorphic to an interval, but it fails second countability, so it is excluded by the library convention.

items.title: A chart domain need not be a Euclidean open set
items.strategy: The domain of a chart is open in the manifold, while the Euclidean open set is its image. Confusing the two swaps the ambient spaces and breaks the coordinate language at the outset.

items.title: Two atlases on the same topological manifold need not have a union atlas
items.strategy: A union is an atlas only when all cross-transition maps are smooth. The cubic coordinate atlas on the line gives a direct counterexample to unconditional union.

items.title: A bijective smooth map need not be a diffeomorphism
items.strategy: The map $x \mapsto x^3$ is smooth and bijective on $\mathbb R$, but its inverse has derivative blowing up at the origin, so smoothness of the inverse is genuinely extra data.

items.title: One smooth transition direction does not guarantee chart compatibility
items.strategy: The same cubic-coordinate example shows that smoothness of one transition map does not force smoothness of its inverse. Both directions must be stated.

items.title: An arbitrary disjoint union of second-countable manifolds need not be second-countable
items.strategy: An uncountable discrete union of one-point manifolds is locally Euclidean and Hausdorff, but every singleton is open, so no countable basis can cover distinct points separately.

title: Smooth Manifolds and Smooth Maps - Examples

items.title: Euclidean spaces and Euclidean open subsets as smooth manifolds
items.strategy: Use the identity chart on $\mathbb R^n$ and its restrictions to open subsets. The A-page standard-structure proposition then supplies the smooth structure immediately.

items.title: The circle from two stereographic charts
items.strategy: Write the north- and south-pole stereographic charts explicitly and compute both transition maps on the overlap. The example witnesses the chart-compatibility definition without importing later regular-level-set machinery.

items.title: The $n$-sphere with its standard smooth atlas
items.strategy: Generalize the two-chart circle construction to the standard stereographic atlas on $S^n$. The transition maps are rational coordinate formulas on $\mathbb R^n \setminus \{0\}$.

items.title: Real projective space from affine charts
items.strategy: Cover projective space by the standard affine patches $x_i \neq 0$ and use the affine coordinate ratios on each patch. The overlap maps are rational and smooth on their domains.

items.title: The torus as a product smooth manifold
items.strategy: Take the product of two circle atlases. The resulting product charts exhibit the torus as a smooth manifold by the A-page product construction.

items.title: A countable disjoint union of lines is a smooth manifold
items.strategy: Apply the countable disjoint-union proposition to a countable family of copies of $\mathbb R$. Each summand contributes its standard chart, and the countability hypothesis is visibly used.

items.title: The long line is locally Euclidean and Hausdorff but not a manifold under the library convention
items.strategy: Invoke the long-line construction and check the only missing axiom: second countability. This is the companion witness for the adopted manifold convention.

items.title: Two noncompatible atlases on the real line
items.strategy: Use the identity chart and the cubic chart on $\mathbb R$. One transition map is $x^3$, while the inverse cube-root map fails to be smooth at $0$.

items.title: A bijective smooth map with nonsmooth inverse
items.strategy: The smooth bijection $x \mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ has inverse $x \mapsto x^{1/3}$, whose first derivative is unbounded at the origin. So bijectivity plus smoothness does not force a diffeomorphism.

items.title: An uncountable disjoint union of points is not second-countable
items.strategy: Every singleton is open in the disjoint-union topology, so a basis must already distinguish uncountably many points. This is the direct witness behind the countability restriction in the A-page disjoint-union theorem.

title: Euclidean Ordinary Differential Equations with Smooth Dependence

items.title: Autonomous ordinary differential equations
The variational equation along an ODE solution
Linear matrix ODEs have unique global solutions on a fixed interval
items.strategy: Extend the coefficient field to an open time interval, view an $n \times n$ matrix as a vector in $\mathbb R^{n^2}$, and apply Picard-Lindelof locally. The Volterra equation, norm-integral estimate, and Gronwall bound control both time directions, and the continuation theorem prevents finite-endpoint breakdown inside the interval.

items.title: A fundamental matrix is invertible
items.strategy: Solve the inverse linear equation and differentiate the product of a candidate inverse with the fundamental matrix. Uniqueness for the identity-valued solution forces the product to stay equal to the identity.

items.title: $C^1$ dependence of solutions on initial data
items.strategy: Difference quotients satisfy a linearized integral equation. The linear comparison estimate and continuous dependence from the published Picard-Lindelof page drive those difference quotients to the solution of the variational equation.

items.title: Smooth dependence of solutions on initial data
items.strategy: Differentiate the Volterra integral equation inductively. At each order the new highest derivative solves an inhomogeneous linear ODE with coefficients built from lower-order derivatives already known to be smooth.

items.title: Smooth dependence of ODE solutions on parameters
items.strategy: Adjoin the parameter as a constant extra variable and reduce the parameter-dependent system to the autonomous initial-data theorem. The common local interval is carried through the augmented system rather than assumed silently.

items.title: A bounded vector field on all of Euclidean space is complete
items.strategy: The integral equation bounds the displacement by the bound on the speed times the elapsed time. A finite maximal endpoint therefore cannot force escape from every compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$, contradicting the published continuation criterion.

items.title: A compactly supported smooth Euclidean vector field is complete
items.strategy: A smooth vector field that vanishes outside a compact subset is bounded on that compact set and zero elsewhere. The previous corollary then gives global existence.

items.title: The fundamental theorem for autonomous smooth ODEs
items.strategy: Combine the published Picard-Lindelof existence and uniqueness theorem with the smooth dependence theorem on a common local interval. The result is stated on the honest open domain of triples where the maximal solution exists.

items.title: The fundamental theorem for nonautonomous smooth ODEs
items.strategy: Adjoin the time variable with $\dot s = 1$ and rewrite the nonautonomous system as an autonomous one in one higher dimension. Apply the autonomous theorem and project back to the original variables.

items.title: The maximal solution domain is open
items.strategy: Take a point where a maximal solution exists, move to the corresponding point on its graph, and apply the local fundamental theorem around that point. The resulting common existence neighborhood propagates existence and smoothness to a whole open set of triples.

items.title: Solutions compose under a change of initial time
items.strategy: Both sides solve the same initial value problem at the intermediate time, so uniqueness on the common domain identifies them. The open-domain proposition ensures the equality is stated exactly where both expressions make sense.

items.title: A smooth Euclidean vector field need not be complete
items.strategy: The scalar equation $\dot x = x^2$ has a smooth right-hand side but the solution from $x(0)=1$ blows up at time $1$. Smoothness does not control growth at infinity.

items.title: Pointwise local existence does not force one global uniform time interval
items.strategy: Uniform time intervals are local in the initial data, not global over all of $\mathbb R^n$. A family of initial conditions moving toward faster and faster blow-up witnesses the failure.

items.title: A maximal ODE solution need not have a closed interval domain
items.strategy: Maximal domains are open intervals because local existence always extends a solution a little away from an interior point. Finite-time blow-up produces a maximal domain of the form $(-\infty,1)$ or $(a,b)$ rather than a closed interval.

items.title: Continuous dependence does not by itself imply differentiable dependence
items.strategy: Differentiable dependence uses derivatives of the vector field and the variational equation. Continuous dependence from Picard-Lindelof is strictly weaker than the smooth-dependence block built on this page.

title: Euclidean Ordinary Differential Equations with Smooth Dependence - Examples

items.title: A constant vector field has translation solutions
items.strategy: Solve $\dot x = v$ explicitly to get $x(t)=x_0+tv$. This is the easiest model of the autonomous fundamental theorem and of completeness.

items.title: A linear system and its fundamental matrix
items.strategy: For $\dot x = Ax$ with constant matrix $A$, the matrix exponential gives the solution operator. This example makes the variational equation and fundamental-matrix language concrete.

items.title: The harmonic oscillator as a first-order system
items.strategy: Rewrite $\ddot q + q = 0$ as a planar linear system and solve it by sine and cosine. The example shows how a classical second-order equation fits the first-order framework used later for geodesics.

items.title: A compactly supported vector field with global solutions
items.strategy: Choose a smooth bump multiple of a constant vector field. Outside the compact support the solution becomes constant, so the completeness corollary is visible directly from the phase portrait.

items.title: Smooth dependence in an ODE with a parameter
items.strategy: Solve $\dot x = \lambda x$ as $x(t)=e^{\lambda t}x_0$ and differentiate the explicit formula in both $x_0$ and $\lambda$. The variational equation matches the derivative formulas exactly.

items.title: A nonautonomous equation made autonomous by adjoining time
items.strategy: Rewrite $\dot x = t x$ as the autonomous system $\dot s = 1$, $\dot x = sx$. The reduction illustrates exactly how the nonautonomous fundamental theorem is proved.
